cause: Peaked 127.5p on 28-Jan-2026, the exact day platinum spot peaked; March 2026 four sessions of -7.6% to -9.2% as the PGM complex broke; grind to 83.2p by 30-Jun as platinum fell to $1,550; then 31-Jul-2026 -10.1% on ~7x median volume on the Q4 operations report — record annual production of 95,885 4E oz but adjusted Group EBITDA -65% q/q to $16.9M because the 4E gross basket fell -25% to $2,299/oz.
top_unverifiable: The host-mine chrome-tailings supply agreements — counterparties, tenure, renewal terms and the split between depleting historical dumps and higher-grade current arisings are disclosed nowhere in the annual report, and the FY25 principal-risks register does not mention feedstock supply at all. SDO owns no ore; the entire business rests on contracts we cannot read.
edge_explainer: Sylvania retreats other miners' chrome tailings in South Africa to recover platinum, palladium and rhodium. Its profit went from $80M to $8M to about $105M in four years, and that swing is essentially all one number: the price of the metal basket. Production rose 43% steadily across the same window and explains almost none of it — hold the metal price flat at last year's level and this year's record output would have earned LESS than last year, because costs rose and the chrome joint venture loses money. Within the last year, the cleanest test: ounces up 4% quarter-on-quarter while the basket price fell 25%, and profit fell 65%. So the stock looks extraordinarily cheap — about 2x operating profit — only because it is being measured at the top of a metal-price cycle. The market pays roughly 4x profit on a metal price about 25% below spot, which is a normal and permanent way to value a commodity producer, not a discount that closes. Buying it is a bet that the long-run platinum basket stays above about $1,750 an ounce. That may be a good bet, but it is a commodity forecast, not the quality-at-a-discount trade this shelf is built to find. The balance sheet is genuinely clean — no debt, cash equal to about a quarter of the market value, a real dividend, a buyback — with three caveats the screen misses: about $9M of that cash would be lost to South African withholding tax on its way to the Bermuda parent; $38.8M is lent to the joint-venture partner whose mine has missed its production target three times running; and for a US taxable holder the 5.3% dividend is taxed as ordinary income, not at the lower qualified rate, which cancels most of the tax advantage the screen credits.
